papers.title_in_file: Towards Robust Benchmarking of Quantum Optimization Algorithms
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, background skim, guidelines skim, Section IV scenario discussions and results text, conclusion
papers.what_it_is: A set of guidelines for fair benchmarking of quantum optimization algorithms against classical solvers, tested on Max-Cut and TSP scenarios.

assertions.value: The authors present a set of guidelines for fair benchmarks of quantum optimization algorithms against classical ones, covering application-specific algorithm choice, benchmark data, a holistic figure of merit and equitable hyperparameter training.
quotes: This paper presents a comprehensive set of guidelines comprising universal steps towards fair benchmarks.
equitable hyperparameter training to eliminate bias towards a particular method
assertions.certainty_reason: The guidelines are the authors' proposal, illustrated on three scenarios.

assertions.value: The authors report that simulated annealing performed best on the small random Max-Cut instances, and that the branch-and-cut solver outperformed the other solvers on the larger real-world-data instances.
assertions.anchor: Section IV scenario 1 discussion; Section V conclusion
quotes: As apparent from the results, SA performs best over all instances.
We have found that SA performs best on the small random instance, while the BNC solver outperforms on the larger problem instances with real-world data.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one benchmark study.
assertions.reader_inference: The small-instance QAOA results come from idealized simulation, so they do not show hardware behavior.

assertions.value: The authors report that, among the QAOA implementations compared for the Travelling Salesperson Problem, the low circuit complexity XY approach works best with regard to time-to-solution.
assertions.anchor: Section IV scenario 3 and Section V conclusion
quotes: For TSP, we compared different QAOA implementations and found that the low circuit complexity XY approach works best with regard to TTS.
The HOBO QAOA is only useful when the number of qubits is limited since TTS increases massively
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from simulated QAOA on small random instances.

assertions.value: The authors state that the proposed steps are not complete but offer a selection of reasonable actions for fair benchmarks.
quotes: Finally, it remains to emphasize that the proposed steps are not complete but offer a selection of reasonable actions for fair benchmarks.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of scope, Section V.

papers.title_in_file: Classical feature map surrogates and metrics for quantum control landscapes
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, setup, numerical example sections skim, barren plateau discussion, conclusions; appendix proofs not read
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper deriving Fourier, Taylor and sinc-kernel surrogate representations of parametrized quantum dynamics landscapes, with bounds and a numerical surrogate benchmark.

assertions.value: The authors prove boundedness of the spectrum and of the cost function derivatives, and show that the landscape is Lipschitz continuous, linking global variation bounds to local Taylor approximation error.
assertions.anchor: Abstract; proofs in Appendices C and D
quotes: We prove boundedness in the spectrum and the cost function derivatives, and discrete symmetries of the coefficients, with implications for learning and simulation.
We further show the landscape is Lipschitz continuous, linking global variation bounds to local Taylor approximation error
assertions.certainty_reason: Proved in the paper; the appendices carry the proofs (Appendices C and D).
assertions.reader_inference: I did not read the appendix proofs.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Lie-Fourier structure yields a new form of polynomial barren plateaux, and that their variance upper bounds constrain the best-case scenario for barren plateaux across quantum systems as set by time, depth and bandwidth limitation.
quotes: This also provides a new form of polynomial barren plateaux originating from the Lie-Fourier structure of the quantum dynamics.
they can be understood as constraints on the best-case scenario for barren plateaux across quantum systems as set by time, depth and bandwidth limitation for their Lie-Fourier expansion.
assertions.certainty_reason: Upper bounds proved in the paper (Lemma 8 and the surrounding discussion).

assertions.value: The authors report that in numerical benchmarks against the other two representations, the sinc kernel was more efficient if the training data set was large enough, and that its inferior performance on small data sets can be greatly improved by reducing the kernel bandwidth.
assertions.anchor: Section IX conclusions; numerical benchmark in the sinc representation section
quotes: In numerical benchmarks against the other two representations, the sinc kernel showed to be more efficient if the training data set is large enough, while its inferior performance on small data sets can be greatly improved by reducing the kernel bandwidth.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical numerical benchmark on the paper's own model systems.

assertions.value: The authors state that the L1 bound is unlikely to be helpful in numerical predictions in general, because of exponential behaviour in the Hilbert space dimension and the number of timesteps.
quotes: Due to the exponential behaviour of r with respect to the dimensionality of the Hilbert space D (which is itself exponential in the number of subsystems) and the number of timesteps N
the L1 bound is unlikely to be helpful in numerical predictions in general, given the results of this analysis.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of their own bound in Section III.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, universality and expressivity sections, discussion; appendix simulations skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A quantum neural network architecture (DIBoM) with a proved universality result, a new fidelity-based expressivity measure and classical-simulation evaluations.

assertions.value: The authors show by a reduction from a known result that the DIBoM can perform universal quantum computation with sufficient depth, and state that it has a flexible number of parameters.
assertions.anchor: Abstract; universality section (reduction from layered single-qubit and CZ circuits)
quotes: achieves provable universality with sufficient parameters.
Additionally, through theoretical analysis, we demonstrated that the DIBoM has the capability of universal quantum computation.
assertions.certainty_reason: Reduction argument in the universality section; it depends on an exponential layer count.
assertions.reader_inference: Universality needs exponentially many layers, so it says little about practical efficiency.

assertions.value: The authors report in a three-qubit task that with 21 layers the DIBoM achieves a fidelity-based expressivity (FBE) exceeding 0.77, whereas the hardware-efficient QNN achieves only around 0.57, and note that the DIBoM has more parameters at the same layer count.
quotes: For instance, with 21 layers, the DIBoM achieves an FBE exceeding 0.77 (where higher values indicate superior performance), whereas the hardware-efficient QNN achieves only around 0.57.
Note however that DIBoM has more parameters than the hardware-efficient QNN with the same number of layers
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from classical simulation of one task.

assertions.value: The authors state that the DIBoM has two potential limitations, trainability and generalizability, and that there is no theoretical guarantee that the DIBoM is trainable.
quotes: There are two potential limitations of the DIBoM: trainability and generalizability.
there is no theoretical guarantee that the DIBoM is trainable
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of limits, Section VII.

assertions.value: The authors state that the classical simulation time is exponential in n, and report that the largest simulation was for n = 8 and took about 1 hour on an 8-core 3.2GHz computer.
quotes: It is worth noting that the computation time is exponential in n, which is a consequence of the classical computation requiring multiple multiplications on density matrices
For the case n = 8, which is the largest simulation we performed, the computation takes about 1 hour on an 8-core 3.2GHz computer.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' statement of the scale of their own simulations.
assertions.reader_inference: All evidence is classical simulation at small qubit counts.

papers.title_in_file: A Differentially Private Quantum Neural Network for Probabilistic Optimal Power Flow
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Section 4.3 theorem statement, Section 5 case study and results, Section 6 conclusion
papers.what_it_is: A differentially private variational quantum circuit model for probabilistic optimal power flow, evaluated against a classical MLP on a modified IEEE 33-bus system.

assertions.value: The authors state that incorporating Gaussian noise into the training process gives the learning algorithm differential privacy with theoretical guarantees, stated as Theorem 1 (Privacy Guarantees).
quotes: By incorporating Gaussian noise into the training process, the learning algorithm achieves
Theorem 1 (Privacy Guarantees).
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1 with proof, Section 4.3.
assertions.reader_inference: The epsilon and delta values are lost in text extraction; I did not verify the proof.

assertions.value: The authors report that without noise the R2 scores are comparable, with the QNN achieving 0.977 and the MLP achieving 0.971, and that under added noise the MLP yields negative R2 scores whereas the QNN maintains positive R2 values.
assertions.anchor: Section 5, Table 3 discussion (voltage magnitude at Node 30)
quotes: In the absence of noise, the obtained R2 scores are comparable, with the QNN achieving 0.977 and the MLP achieving 0.971.
the MLP yields negative R2 scores, whereas the QNN maintains positive R2 values
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on one simulated system.
assertions.reader_inference: Noise-scale values are lost in extraction; they are in Table 3 of the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that, compared to classical NNs, the QNN demonstrates superior approximation accuracy while reducing the number of parameters by 90%.
quotes: Compared to classical NNs, the QNN demonstrates superior approximation accuracy while reducing the number of parameters by 90%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one comparison against one MLP.

assertions.value: The authors state that the experiments use the modified IEEE 33-bus power distribution system and that the QNN output is the voltage magnitude at one node because of the qubit limitation in the NISQ era.
quotes: Numerical experiments are conducted on the modified IEEE 33-bus power distribution system.
The output is the voltage magnitude at node i due to the qubit limitation in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' statement of their experimental setup, Section 5.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Neural Ordinary and Partial Differential Equations
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, contents, cost-of-gradient-estimation discussion in Section IV D, numerical examples text in Section V, Summary and Outlook; appendix proofs not read
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper introducing continuous-time quantum neural ODE and PDE models with quantum gradient-estimation algorithms and small simulated demonstrations.

assertions.value: The authors introduce a framework of Quantum Neural Ordinary and Partial Differential Equations that permits gradient estimation via an adjoint-state method.
quotes: This formalism permits gradient estimation via an adjoint-state method, facilitating efficient learning of quantum dynamics
assertions.certainty_reason: The framework is the paper's own definition, Sections III and IV.

assertions.value: The authors state that their quantum algorithms achieve efficient gradient computation that would otherwise be intractable on classical devices, and that their scaling discussion is heuristic with a fuller analysis left for future work.
quotes: achieving efficient gradient computation that would otherwise be intractable on classical devices.
Although heuristic, this discussion already outlines the promising scaling of our approach; a more comprehensive mathematical analysis is left for future work.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors call the supporting discussion heuristic.
assertions.reader_inference: The advantage holds only where the Hamiltonian is hard to simulate classically and a quantum device is assumed.

assertions.value: The authors report simulation results for Hamiltonian learning from observable data that they say demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of their approach, using smaller systems because of the cost of classically emulating mixed states.
quotes: Due to the relatively higher cost of classically emulating mixed states, we consider smaller systems for this example.
Simulation results are shown in Figure 5a, demonstrating the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach.
assertions.certainty_reason: Small classical simulations by the authors.

assertions.value: The authors state that it remains to investigate whether their complexity analysis is tight, and that each application requires more in-depth study left to future work.
quotes: It remains to investigate whether the above analysis is tight for some parameters
Each of these applications requires more in-depth study in their own right for specific scenarios, and we leave this to future work for specific models.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of limits, Sections IV D and VI.

papers.title_in_file: Experimental quantum reservoir computing with a circuit quantum electrodynamics system
papers.what_it_is: A hardware experiment implementing quantum reservoir computing with a transmon coupled to a resonator, with classification tasks and Kerr-effect simulations.

assertions.value: The authors report a proof-of-concept realization of quantum reservoir computing with a single transmon coupled to a readout resonator.
quotes: we show that even with a circuit quantum electrodynamics system as simple as a single transmon coupled to a readout resonator, we can implement a proof-of-concept realization of quantum reservoir computing.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one experimental device.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the sine and square waveform classification task, 20 measured features give 99.8% accuracy on the test set, and the eight most informative features still give 99.5 % accuracy.
quotes: With 20 measured features, yielding 21 output neurons including the bias, we find that the prediction on the test set matches the target with 99.8% accuracy.
we still achieve 99.5 % accuracy, as shown in Figure 3(c).
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on one task and one device.

assertions.value: The authors state that classical reservoir computing requires at least twenty-five classical features to achieve comparable performance, and describe this as consistent with previous simulations.
quotes: where at least twenty-five classical features are required to achieve comparable performance, and is consistent with previous simulations [19].
assertions.certainty_reason: A comparison attributed to prior simulation work, not run in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that all training and testing data were acquired within a single continuous measurement session with stationary dynamics, and that the long-term stability of trained reservoirs has not been systematically investigated.
quotes: In the present work, all training and testing data are acquired within a single continuous measurement session, during which the system dynamics remain stationary and the trained readout remains valid.
the long-term stability of trained reservoirs has not been systematically investigated.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of limits, Section VI.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Section 1 introduction with informal theorems and directions for future work; formal proofs not read
papers.what_it_is: A learning-theory paper on classical verification of untrusted quantum learners for agnostic parity and Fourier-sparse learning, with a new quantum data access model.

assertions.value: The authors prove that agnostic quantum parity and Fourier-sparse learning can be efficiently verified by a classical verifier with only random example or statistical query access, and state that the separation is unconditional for SQ access and conditional on the hardness of Learning Parity with Noise for random example access.
assertions.anchor: Abstract; Section 1.2 Theorem 2 (informal), proved in Section 6
quotes: Moreover, we prove that agnostic quantum parity and Fourier-sparse learning can be efficiently verified by a classical verifier with only random example or statistical query access.
This separation is unconditional for SQ access and conditional on the hardness of Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) for random example access.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 2, proved in Section 6.
assertions.reader_inference: The result holds for a promised distribution class and a new data access model that needs quantum data.

assertions.value: The authors state that Theorem 1, proved in Section 5, constitutes the first general progress on distributional agnostic quantum learning with respect to uniform input marginal, and give efficient quantum learning algorithms for parities and Fourier-sparse functions.
quotes: Theorem 1, proved in Section 5, constitutes the first general progress on distributional agnostic quantum learning w.r.t. uniform input marginal.
we give efficient quantum learning algorithms for these tasks.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1 and Theorem 5, proved in Section 5.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum sample complexity of distribution-independent distributional agnostic learning from these quantum examples does not improve upon the classical sample complexity, up to logarithmic factors.
quotes: does not improve upon the classical sample complexity, up to logarithmic factors.
quantum mixture-of-superpositions examples do not lead to sample complexity improvements over classical data
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 3, lower bound proved in Section 7.

assertions.value: The authors state that it remains unclear whether mixture-of-superpositions examples are strictly more powerful than standard quantum superposition examples.
quotes: it remains unclear whether mixture-of-superpositions examples are indeed strictly more powerful than standard quantum superposition examples.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of an open question, Section 1.5.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Section VII hardware results, Section VIII, Section IX discussion; parameter-setting, routing and error-mitigation sections skimmed
papers.what_it_is: An approach that uses QAOA samples from noisy quantum hardware as warm starts for classical Max-Cut and MIS heuristics, reporting runtime improvements by a Q-factor metric.

assertions.value: The authors report that quantum warm starts significantly improve classical heuristics such as tabu search where those rely on random initializations, with a Q-factor speedup exceeding 1000 in certain cases.
assertions.anchor: Section IX Discussion and Conclusions; Section I
quotes: The speedup, as measured by the Q-factor, reaches values exceeding 1000

the introduction of quantum warm starts significantly improves the performance of classical heuristics like tabu search in instances where classical optimization algorithms rely on random initializations
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from emulation and IBM hardware runs on selected instances.
assertions.reader_inference: The baseline is random initialization of one tabu-search heuristic.

assertions.value: The authors state that their runtime metrics did not take into account the runtime required to obtain the QAOA samples, and that their runtime comparison is not a fair final comparison.
assertions.anchor: Section VII C 2 and Section IX
quotes: Our runtime metrics did not take into account the runtime required to obtain the QAOA samples
this runtime comparison does not include the time taken to generate the warm starts or random samples in either case, meaning it is not a fair final comparison.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of a limit of their metric, Sections VII and IX.
assertions.reader_inference: The reported speedups are therefore not end-to-end wall-clock speedups.

assertions.value: The authors state that several questions remain to be answered before the approach can be said to have delivered a genuine quantum advantage.
quotes: Despite this, several questions remain to be answered before this approach can be said to have delivered a genuine quantum advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of scope, Section IX.

assertions.value: The authors state that their study focused on problem sizes up to 55 qubits on IBM hardware, and report that as problem sizes grow, noise from the device begins to take over as circuit depth increases.
quotes: our study focused on problem sizes up to 55 qubits on IBM hardware.
As the problem sizes get larger, we see noise from the device begin to take over as the circuit depth increases
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' statement of their own experimental scope, Section IX.
